title: Frontend shell: layout, routing and design tokens
goal: Set up the ApplyTrack Angular app with a clean layout, lazy routes and a small design system.

concepts: Angular + Tailwind in web/; proxy to the API in development
App shell: header, sidebar (desktop) / bottom nav (mobile), content area
Lazy-loaded feature routes: auth, applications, dashboard, settings
Design tokens with Tailwind theme (colours per status, spacing, radius)
Shared UI components: button, input, badge, card, empty state, skeleton
Dark mode with the class strategy

build.task: In applytrack/web: create the Angular app with Tailwind and proxy.conf.json to the API. Build the shell (responsive: sidebar at md and up, bottom nav on mobile), lazy routes (/login, /register, /applications, /applications/:id, /dashboard, /settings) with placeholder pages, a 404 page, and shared components in src/app/ui/: Button (variants and loading state), TextField (label, error), StatusBadge (one colour per status), Card, EmptyState and Skeleton. Add a dark-mode toggle saved in localStorage. Build a /styleguide route showing every shared component.
acceptance: Responsive shell works at 375 px and 1280 px
All routes lazy-loaded (check separate chunks in the build output)
Six shared UI components, each used on /styleguide
StatusBadge colours defined once, in the theme
Dark mode toggle persists and covers every component
Keyboard focus is visible on all interactive elements

hints: Define status colours once: a map in one file like { Wishlist: 'bg-slate-100 text-slate-700', Applied: 'bg-blue-100 text-blue-700', ... } used by StatusBadge and the dashboard.
Use Tailwind's @custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *)); and toggle the 'dark' class on <html>.
A /styleguide page is a great review tool: you see every component state at once, and it impresses in interviews.
proof: Commit with the shell, routes, shared UI and styleguide.

explainBack.q: Why build shared UI components before the feature pages?
How do you know the routes are lazy-loaded?
lookFor: separate chunk files in the build output
Network tab loads chunks on navigation

lastHintExplanation: Shared components (buttons, fields, badges) give every page the same look and behaviour, and make feature pages faster to build. A style fix happens in one place. Lazy routes appear as separate chunk files in the ng build output and load in the Network tab only when you navigate to them.

dsa.note: New pattern. JavaScript has no built-in heap: write a small MinHeap class (push, pop, peek, size), or sort for small inputs. Keep a min-heap of size k.

title: Auth pages and session handling
goal: Give ApplyTrack a polished sign-up and login experience with robust session handling.

concepts: AuthService with signals; restoring the session on startup (provideAppInitializer)
Auth and error interceptors; authGuard and guestGuard (logged-in users skip /login)
Showing server errors on forms (409 duplicate email, 401 invalid login)
Password strength hints and a show/hide toggle
Accessible forms: labels, aria-describedby for errors, autocomplete attributes

build.task: In applytrack/web: login and register pages using your shared components and reactive forms; server errors mapped to the right field or a form-level message; password show/hide and strength hint; correct autocomplete attributes (email, current-password, new-password). AuthService restores the session at startup via /api/auth/me before routing (no flash of the login page). Interceptors attach the token and handle 401 by logging out and redirecting with returnUrl. guestGuard sends logged-in users from /login to /applications. Add a Settings page to edit your name and change your password.
acceptance: Register, login, logout and settings work end to end
Reload on a private page stays on that page (no login flash)
Server errors appear in the right place on the form
autocomplete attributes let the browser's password manager work
Forms are fully usable with keyboard and screen reader labels

hints: provideAppInitializer(() => inject(AuthService).restoreSession()): Angular waits for the returned promise before the first navigation.
Map a 409 on register to the email field: this.form.controls.email.setErrors({ server: 'This email is already registered' }).

Link errors to inputs:

...
proof: Commit with auth pages, session handling and settings.

explainBack.q: Why restore the session in an app initializer instead of in a component?
What do the autocomplete attributes do for the user?

lastHintExplanation: If the session is restored after routing starts, the guard sees 'logged out' for a moment and bounces the user to /login. An app initializer makes Angular wait until /auth/me answers. autocomplete='current-password' and 'new-password' tell password managers what each field is, so they fill and save credentials correctly.

dsa.note: Repeatedly take the two largest. A max-heap is ideal; sorting each round is fine for small inputs.

title: Applications list: filters, search and two views
goal: Build the main screen: a fast, filterable applications list with table and board views.

concepts: An ApplicationsStore with signals: list, meta, loading, error, query
Query params as the single source of truth for filters, sort and page
Debounced search; multi-select status filter; date range
Table view (desktop) and Kanban board view by status
Drag and drop between columns with the Angular CDK (calls the status endpoint)
Optimistic updates with rollback on error

build.task: In applytrack/web: /applications with a filter bar (search, status multi-select, applied date range, sort) fully synced to query params; a table view with pagination for desktop and a card list on mobile; a board view (toggle saved in localStorage) with one column per status where dragging a card changes its status via PATCH /status, optimistically, rolling back with a toast on error. Loading skeletons, an empty state with a 'Add your first application' button, and a 'No results — clear filters' state.
acceptance: All filters, sort and page live in the URL; reload and back button work
Table/cards and board views both work; the view choice persists
Drag and drop changes status on the server; failure rolls back with a toast
Distinct loading, empty and no-results states
Keyboard users can change status without dragging (e.g. a status menu on each card)

hints: Read query params as signals with withComponentInputBinding(), or toSignal(route.queryParamMap). Update them with router.navigate([], { queryParams, queryParamsHandling: 'merge' }).
Optimistic move: const prev = app.status; store.setStatus(id, next); try { await api.changeStatus(id, next) } catch { store.setStatus(id, prev); toast.error('Could not move application') }
Drag and drop alone isn't accessible. Add a small 'Move to…' dropdown on each card as the keyboard alternative.
proof: Commit with the list, board and filters, plus a short screen recording (GIF) in the PR or README.

explainBack.q: Explain optimistic updates and the risk they bring.
lookFor: UI can briefly show wrong state

explainBack.q: Why provide a non-drag way to change status?

lastHintExplanation: An optimistic update changes the UI immediately and assumes the server will agree, which makes the board feel instant. The cost is that you must undo the change cleanly if the request fails. Drag and drop needs a mouse or precise touch, so a 'Move to…' menu keeps the feature usable with a keyboard or screen reader.

dsa.note: Count with a Map, then keep the k most frequent with a heap (or bucket sort by frequency for O(n)).

title: Application form and detail page
goal: Build the add/edit form and a rich detail page with timeline, interviews and contacts.

concepts: One reusable form component for create and edit
Typed reactive forms with nested FormArrays (contacts)
Unsaved-changes guard (canDeactivate)
Detail page: info, status timeline from history, interviews, contacts, notes
Dates and times: displaying in the user's locale; sending ISO strings

build.task: In applytrack/web: an ApplicationForm component used by /applications/new and /applications/:id/edit (company, role, job URL with validation, location, salary range, source select, applied date, notes), with server-side errors shown and a canDeactivate guard for unsaved changes. A detail page /applications/:id with a header (company, role, StatusBadge, quick status change), a status timeline from history, an interviews section (add/edit/delete, upcoming highlighted), a contacts section, and notes. Delete the application with a confirmation dialog (use a custom dialog, not window.confirm).
acceptance: Same form component handles create and edit
Unsaved-changes guard prompts before leaving a dirty form
Detail page shows timeline, interviews and contacts, all editable
Dates displayed in en-IN format; interviews shown in local time
Delete uses an accessible custom dialog (focus trapped, Esc closes)

hints: Edit mode: if the route has an id, load the application and form.patchValue(app); on save, call update instead of create.
canDeactivate: export const unsavedChangesGuard: CanDeactivateFn<{ isDirty(): boolean }> = (c) => !c.isDirty() || confirmDialog.open('Discard changes?');
The native <dialog> element with showModal() gives you focus trapping and Esc to close for free.
proof: Commit with the form, detail page and dialog.

explainBack.q: How does one form component handle both create and edit?
Why use the native <dialog> instead of window.confirm or a plain div?

lastHintExplanation: The form only needs to know whether it has an existing application: if so, it patches the values in and saves with update, otherwise with create. The native <dialog> with showModal() traps focus, closes on Esc and is announced as a dialog by screen readers. window.confirm can't be styled and blocks the whole page.

dsa.note: Keep a max-heap of size k by distance (or sort for simplicity, then improve).

title: Dashboard: stats and charts
goal: Turn your stats endpoint into a clear, accessible dashboard.

concepts: Stat cards: total, active, interviews this week, offers, response rate
Charts with Chart.js: applications per week (bar) and status breakdown
Accessible charts: titles, colour plus labels, a data table alternative
Upcoming interviews list
Refreshing stats after changes elsewhere (shared store or refetch on navigation)

build.task: In applytrack/web: /dashboard with five stat cards; a bar chart of applications per week (last 8 weeks); a status breakdown (horizontal bar or doughnut) using the same status colours as the badges; an 'Upcoming interviews' list for the next 7 days linking to each application; and a 'Needs follow-up' list (Applied more than 14 days ago with no status change). Each chart has a title, a visually hidden data table for screen readers and a 'Show as table' toggle. Destroy charts on component destroy. Make the dashboard the default route after login.
acceptance: Five stat cards with correct numbers (check against the database)
Both charts render with consistent status colours
Upcoming interviews and needs-follow-up lists work and link through
Charts have accessible table alternatives
No chart memory leaks when navigating away and back

hints: Create the chart in an effect or afterNextRender once the canvas exists, keep the instance, and call chart.destroy() in ngOnDestroy (or with DestroyRef.onDestroy).
'Needs follow-up' is easier on the server: add GET /api/applications?status=Applied&staleDays=14, or a dedicated stats field.
Use the same status colour map as StatusBadge, converted to hex for Chart.js.
proof: Commit with the dashboard and a screenshot in the README.

explainBack.q: How did you make the charts accessible?
Why destroy Chart.js instances when the component is destroyed?

lastHintExplanation: Charts are images to a screen reader, so an equivalent data table, clear titles and labels (not colour alone) make the data available to everyone. Chart.js attaches listeners and keeps references to its canvas; if you don't destroy it, every visit to the dashboard leaks another chart, and re-using the canvas throws errors.

dsa.note: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half; balance their sizes. Hard: understand it even if you don't finish.

title: Bug bash and week review
goal: Use ApplyTrack like a real user, find bugs and rough edges, and fix the important ones.

concepts: Bug bash: structured exploratory testing
Writing good bug reports: steps, expected, actual, environment, severity
Triage: fix now, fix later, won't fix
Testing edge cases: long text, empty data, slow network, expired session, mobile
DevTools network throttling and offline mode

resources.title: How to write a good bug report (Atlassian)

build.task: Run a 90-minute bug bash on ApplyTrack with the checklist: very long company names, 200 applications (bulk seed), empty account, slow 3G, offline, expired token mid-form, two tabs open, 375 px width, keyboard only, dark mode, and refreshing on every route. Log every issue as a GitHub issue with steps, expected, actual and severity. Fix all high-severity issues today, each in its own commit referencing the issue. Ask one friend or family member to try adding an application without help and note where they hesitate. Write week21-notes.md.
acceptance: Every checklist item tested
At least 8 well-written bug issues with severity labels
All high-severity bugs fixed and closed from commits
Notes from one real user test
week21-notes.md lists what's fixed and what's left

hints: Bulk seed 200 applications with generate_series in a seed script so you can test pagination and performance.
Long text breaks layouts: use truncate or line-clamp with a title attribute, and min-w-0 on flex children.
Watching someone else use your app for 10 minutes finds more UX problems than an hour of testing it yourself.
proof: Link to your issues list filtered by the 'bug' label.

explainBack.q: Pick your best bug report and explain why it's good.
What did the real user test reveal that you hadn't noticed?

lastHintExplanation: A good bug report lets someone else reproduce the problem without asking you anything: exact steps, what should have happened, what did happen, and where (browser, screen size). Users who didn't build the app don't know your shortcuts, so they reveal confusing labels and hidden actions within minutes.

dsa.note: Merge k sorted lists with a min-heap of the current heads. Then re-solve Top K Frequent Elements.
